Analysis

Theme

The vocabulary of war changed

"Aggression" peaked in 1975 to 1987, mostly about South Africa, then all but disappeared. "Breach of the peace" was found for only four wars, the last in 1990. "Threat to the peace" became the routine trigger: 2% of resolutions in the founding era, 55% today.

Article 39 of the Charter lets the Council act once it finds a "threat to the peace, breach of the peace, or act of aggression". The three terms have had very different lives in the documents.

Aggression: a Cold War word

28 resolutions speak of an "act of aggression". The states named in them: South Africa 19, Southern Rhodesia 6, Israel 2, Portugal 1. After 1988 the phrase appears only once, in 984 (1995), about hypothetical nuclear attacks. No adopted resolution has found an act of aggression since, including over Kuwait in 1990 and Ukraine since 2022. Resolution 2774 (2025) speaks of the "Russian Federation-Ukraine conflict".

Breach of the peace: open invasions only

The Council has found a breach of the peace in only 6 resolutions, about four wars between states.

  • 82 (1950) Calling upon the North Korean authorities to withdraw their armed forces to the 38th parallel
  • 83 (1950) Assistance to the Republic of Korea
  • 84 (1950) The Korean question and a unified command under the United States
  • 502 (1982) Demanding withdrawal of Argentine forces from the Falkland Islands (Malvinas)
  • 598 (1987) Requesting the Secretary-General to dispatch observers to supervise the cease-fire between Iraq and the Islamic Republic of Iran
  • 660 (1990) Iraqi invasion of Kuwait

Threat to the peace: the all-purpose key

The first finding is Palestine in 1948 (54 (1948)). Since 2001 the Council has also applied it to terrorism (1373 (2001)), weapons of mass destruction (1540 (2004)) and Ebola (2177 (2014)). It now appears in 55% of resolutions, because a threat finding is what opens Chapter VII.
